title: Aggettivi e Accordo
subtitle: Adjectives must match the noun they describe in gender and number.
objectives: Make -o/-a adjectives agree in gender and number
Use -e adjectives, which don't change for gender
Place adjectives correctly before or after the noun

content.intro: An Italian adjective isn't fixed — it changes its ending to match the noun it describes, exactly like the article does.
content.explanation: Most adjectives end in -o in the masculine singular and change to -a, -i, -e to agree with the noun. A second group ends in -e for both masculine and feminine singular, changing only for plural. Most descriptive adjectives follow the noun (una casa grande), while a small set of very common adjectives (bello, buono, grande, piccolo, giovane, vecchio...) can also come before it, sometimes with a slightly different nuance.

rules.heading: b) -e adjectives (two forms)
rules.body:
• sing. (m. or f.) -e: un ragazzo intelligente, una ragazza intelligente
  • pl. (m. or f.) -i: ragazzi intelligenti, ragazze intelligenti

rules.heading: c) Position
rules.body:
• Most adjectives follow the noun: un libro interessante
  • A short list (bello, brutto, buono, cattivo, grande, piccolo, giovane, vecchio, nuovo) often precede it: una bella giornata

examples.en: We have a nice small house.

commonMistakes.why: The adjective must agree with the feminine noun ragazza, so it needs the -a ending.
-e adjectives take -i for the plural, not -o — interessante is not an -o/-a adjective.
Bianco needs a spelling adjustment (c→ch) to keep the hard "k" sound before the plural -e.

items.explanation: Feminine plural takes -e.

items.explanation: -e adjectives share one singular form across both genders.

items.statement: Adjectives never change their ending, regardless of the noun.
items.explanation: Adjectives must agree with the noun's gender and number.

items.statement: Simpatico becomes simpatici in the masculine plural.
items.explanation: Masculine plural of -o/-a adjectives takes -i.

items.statement: Most Italian adjectives come before the noun they describe.
items.explanation: Most adjectives follow the noun; only a short, common set can also precede it.

items.explanation: Bianche keeps the hard "k" sound thanks to the added h.

items.explanation: -e adjectives have only two forms: -e (singular) and -i (plural).

items.statement: Grande is an example of an -e adjective.
items.explanation: Grande keeps the same singular form for both genders, like any -e adjective.

items.statement: Adjective agreement depends only on the noun's gender, never its number.
items.explanation: Agreement depends on both gender and number.

items.statement: Piccolo, grande and buono are among the adjectives that can precede the noun.
items.explanation: These are part of the short, common set that can come before the noun.

summary: -o/-a adjectives have four forms: -o, -a, -i, -e, matching the noun's gender and number.
-e adjectives have only two forms: -e (singular, both genders) and -i (plural, both genders).
Most adjectives follow the noun; a short, common set can also precede it.
